facts: I estimate that I started seriously experimenting with AI programming tools around this time in the previous year, choosing the six-to-twelve-month range.

At the original interview I used Claude Code almost exclusively, having obtained access in December. I considered it the best available tool. My repositories still automatically trigger GitHub Copilot reviews on pull requests, but I do not find those reviews particularly useful and otherwise rarely use Copilot.

I mainly program in Go using JetBrains GoLand. Its Copilot integration only autocompletes the end of text, which I dislike and retain because I have not figured out how to disable it. I rarely write code in the IDE now, mostly reading code there, because I find Claude Code and newer models so capable.

I mainly use Claude Code to retrieve information rather than program, integrating it through MCP with GitHub, Confluence, Grafana and Kubernetes. I work as a lead software engineer in a company with roughly 5,000 engineers and thousands of repositories. Much of my job is clarifying open-ended business problems, searching multiple sources, mentoring implementers and writing architecture decision records. Claude can locate relevant code or old Confluence pages, so I describe it as Google on steroi

When I perform the individual activities, I use Claude Code very often for code generation, debugging (with a dedicated debugging skill), understanding unfamiliar code, refactoring (although I rarely refactor), and writing tests as part of normal code generation. For documentation I rate AI use between sometimes and often: I struggle to obtain satisfactory writing, have created several skills including one imitating my writing style, and still sometimes write manually. I use AI very often for in

For a repository task in the week before the original interview I had written a Markdown solution proposal with Claude. Using terminal and IDE, I opened a new chat and requested brainstorming using the Superpowers brainstorming skill. Claude read the proposal, gathered context from GitHub and other sources, articulated its understanding and proposed about three approaches. I corrected inaccuracies and iterated until we agreed on the problem and solution. Claude then wrote a Markdown specificatio

Rather than receiving ordinary tickets, I typically write Jira tickets for others. My manager gives me vague problems, and I bridge business and engineering to clarify them and create tasks. In the recent implementation example I wrote the solution proposal for myself.

In my general work I write code sometimes, making at least one code commit per week. I review code very often, daily, primarily AI-generated code; reviews of colleagues' code alone would be rare. I rate bug fixing and debugging sometimes.

I rarely run tests personally because they are part of Claude's workflow, but tests run on my machine often. I rate specification very often, including architecture decision records, especially over the preceding week. I do documentation sometimes and learn very often, daily, partly because AI changes rapidly.
Of my frequent activities, specification takes the most time, followed by code review and learning in that order.

On Monday and the day before the original interview I wrote an approximately 600-line Markdown request for comments, or solution proposal. Our mainframe exposes an HTTP API limited to 25 requests per second. We proposed a materialization gateway exposing an HTTP API using data from roughly 20–25 Kafka topics rather than directly fetching from the mainframe, to avoid that rate limit. We agreed on the overall direction in a Friday meeting, then I spent both Monday and Tuesday writing the proposal.

I rarely work with code I did not write because organizational silos make teams reluctant to enter one another's repositories and I am busy. Claude Code makes unfamiliar repositories easier to explore but it is still difficult. I would like to do more cross-team code work.

A colleague asked me to record AI success stories because management wanted expensive AI tooling used sensibly. In late February I joined my current project, which had about 15 engineers, several established repositories and had run since June. I asked Claude to explore the repositories, explain the technology stack, current work, code bases and business problems and how they relate. I found AI helpful for onboarding.

On Saturday March 14, despite not normally working weekends, I was trying to authenticate to a company API requiring two keys and complex documentation. I asked Claude to read its specification and determine how to authenticate. During a GitHub search Claude unexpectedly found that a second public domain exposed the API without authentication, which I considered a serious security breach. Because ownership was unclear, Claude found the appropriate repository and its five most recent committers i

I have read studies suggesting perceived AI productivity gains can exceed measured gains and sometimes AI makes people slower. Personally I feel my gains are substantial, especially information retrieval: finding a repository manually via GitHub searches might previously have taken me five to ten minutes, whereas Claude can do it almost immediately.

To validate generated code I first inspect whether tests cover important behavior and pass, then inspect code style, abstractions and separation of concerns. If tests fail I request another iteration. I manually review code and often ask Claude to spawn a separate review sub-agent because its fresh context provides an independent perspective, like a colleague reviewing code I wrote manually.

I frequently use sub-agents to review Claude's outputs, including my recent gateway solution proposal. For example, I asked Claude to source a claim that a Kafka topic would contain 30 GB of messages, and it linked the Grafana metric. I also use an in-house AI review system as a further layer more separated from the original context.

I would like research on whether AI actually improves measured productivity and whether AI can review code better than humans. I feel traditional human review is under pressure from rapidly increasing code output and suspect AI may already be better. Human feedback previously could take half a day and two or three iterations, while Claude can review in ten minutes. I think a reliable AI-only review process could substantially increase velocity, although I do not think industry is fully there yet
